source.version_note: Published PLOS ONE 19(2), e0292944, 29 February 2024; received 25 January 2023, accepted 2 October 2023. Six samples across Studies 1a, 1b, 1c, 2, 3 and 4, despite the abstract listing selected recruited samples. Main article plus public S1 Appendix DOCX read.
source.verification_method: All 34 supplied pages, five main tables, seven main figures and 63 references read. Public S1 Appendix read completely: three supplementary tables, all participant instructions and all three embedded images. Crossref verifies main identity, Longoni, Promberger and Soltan metadata; indexed Wiley metadata verifies Prahl’s journal. Linked repository code/data and registration contents were not independently accessed, and no clinical performance or raw analysis was reproduced.

citation.title: Who should decide how limited healthcare resources are prioritized? Autonomous technology as a compelling alternative to humans

reading.source_scope_note: UK online public samples describe and rate hypothetical human/autonomous referral centres. A scale-development/confirmation sequence and repeated-profile judgment tasks measure perceived qualities and appropriateness, not real clinical performance, actual patient referrals, safety or deployment. Uniqueness neglect is discussed from a cited original rather than independently manipulated here.

supplement.title: S1 Appendix: supplementary results and participant instructions
supplement.coverage: All 593 nonempty text paragraphs, including every table cell, grouped into three complete tables and instructions; all three embedded images visually read. No page count invented for the DOCX.

access_limits: Linked raw data/model scripts and registration contents were not independently inspected. Model-unit ambiguities, software version and exact test tails remain unverified; no raw numerical repair.

The original Longoni medical-AI study and other cited psychology/clinical studies were not independently fully read as part of this review. Identity checks are not additional independent-paper credit.
No clinical sample, observed health outcome, deployed algorithm benchmark, regulatory audit or implementation of the suggested adoption strategy is supplied.

study.participants: Reported recruited→retained participations: 1a 50→50; 1b 800→771 (27 attention and two speed exclusions); 1c 619→589 (30 attention); 2 371→300 (71 comprehension/attention); 3 181→153 (28 comprehension); 4 378→310 (68 comprehension). Total 2399 recruited/2173 retained participations, not verified unique people across Prolific samples. UK adults, prior-study/approval filters; female shares 82%,69%,52%,54%,50%,49%. Samples are not patients or clinicians and healthcare work experience is not controlled.
study.qualitative: Study 1a asks four open questions about required qualities, ACP advantages, human advantages and barriers. Categories are derived by one coder from a random half of responses and checked by another on the same half; kappa .60/.60/.60/.65. This is a codebook-based inductive analysis with limited calibration, not an independent holdout validation or a single objective taxonomy.
study.qualitative_counts: Table 1 totals are sums of reference occasions across questions, e.g. communication 12+0+14+16 = 42. Dividing 42 by 50 does not establish 42 distinct people across all questions. Reassurance has eight mentions, 16% of 50, not the printed 39%. Its inclusion also contradicts the stated at-least-25% category rule. The same people describe both agents; within-person dependence matters for category comparisons and a paired analysis should be specified.
study.scale_development: Study 1b begins with 35 items, performs separate oblique EFAs for human/ACP ratings (initially four/seven factors), then selects 19 items and retains four factors: eight agentic/communication, five emotional experience, three bias-free and three error-free. Same-sample item selection is exploratory; the human fourth eigenvalue is .92 and retained partly to match the ACP structure. Some emotional/agency cross-loading remains.
study.factor_sign: Table 3 contrasts positive human and negative ACP bias-free loadings. EFA factor orientation is arbitrary: reversing a factor and its loadings leaves the fitted covariance unchanged. Opposite signs alone do not establish opposite psychological poles or reversed item meaning. S3’s separate CFA loadings are positive for both agents. Mean item ratings and tested differences remain interpretable independently of the arbitrary sign.
study.confirmatory_validation: Study 1c is a separate 589-person CFA sample, 288 human/301 ACP, using correlated four-factor models. Human chi²(146) = 310.43, CFI .941, RMSEA .063; ACP chi²(146) = 330.95, CFI .923, RMSEA .065. This provides independent structural evidence and must not be omitted. RMSEA values are below .08, not exceeding it; fit is not ideal under the paper’s stricter .95/.05 benchmarks. Separate acceptable fits do not establish cross-agent measurement invariance or clinical validity.
study.perceived_capabilities: Study 1b human/ACP overall ratings 3.87/3.05. Human-minus-ACP contrasts: agency +1.34, emotional experience +3.41, bias-free −.56, error-free −.90, reported p < .001. These are perceived capacities, not verified machine impartiality, accuracy or consciousness. Agency here includes communication/flexibility; experience mixes feeling and compassion.
study.capability_permissibility: Human/ACP permissibility means 3.95/2.93. Results report agency association b = .24, p < .001, and an ACP simple slope .32, p < .001, versus uncertain human slope .07, p = .484. The discussion’s blanket no-association statement must therefore be narrowed. The participant-level mean-permissibility outcome and claimed repeated-measure random intercept require code clarification; no invalid model is asserted from text alone.
study.study2_design: A fictional independent panel awards one-to-five stars on four qualities for 40 centres. Participants receive a random 40-profile subset of a generated 50-profile set, judge appropriateness on 1–5, then rate importance and plausibility. Profiles are near-orthogonal with balanced ranges and order. No centres or panel assessments are real, and a star is not a calibrated error rate or clinical endpoint.
study.study2_results: Random-intercept/slopes profile model coefficients: error-free .40, bias-free .31, agency .22, experience .14; adjacent Wald contrasts are significant. Human mean 2.89 versus ACP 2.58; condition×quality interactions are uncertain. At other qualities = three stars, fitted ACP means for bias-free four/five stars 2.91/3.22 and error-free 3.00/3.39 are compared to human three-star mean 2.90. Crossing a fitted point benchmark is not formal equivalence/noninferiority; confidence in the difference needs its own interval.
study.adjustment_and_registration: The paper discloses Study 1b’s ANOVA→mixed-model change and Study 2’s plausibility-covariate change from the registered plan. Plausibility is measured after the judgment task and can be treatment-affected or influenced by prior responses; adjustment is not automatic control of a pretreatment confound or unique causal mediation. Registration contents/timing were not independently verified.
study.study3: Within-person relative profiles drop emotional experience and compare ACP performance to a fixed human reference on three qualities, with 40 near-orthogonal trials and 7-point judgments from human-favored −3 to ACP-favored +3. Slopes agency .47, bias-free .45, error-free .56; error-free exceeds agency (Wald 9.11, p = .003), while agency versus bias-free is uncertain (.62,p = .431). Equal-performance intercept −.24 favors humans. Better/much-better ACP profiles have positive fitted relative preferences. These are stated judgments, not actual delegation or patient choices.
study.study4: 159 low/151 high autonomy participants compare fixed-rule versus self-created-rule referral centres; agency wording is changed to remove communication. Preference weighting/interactions remain uncertain, with overall equal-performance intercept around −.27 and slopes .45/.47/.57. Likelihood ratings do respond: high autonomy implies more perceived agency (+.65), less bias-free (−.80) and less error-free (−.42) than low autonomy, reported significant. This concerns expectations, not measured error/bias of autonomous systems; nonsignificant preference effects are not equivalence.
study.scope: The tasks concern nonemergency waiting-list coordination such as physiotherapy, despite an introduction invoking emergency triage and COVID pressures. No actual emergency resource allocation, fairness outcome, treatment quality, cost-effectiveness or clinically safe autonomous threshold is tested. Favorable performance information can rationally change preferences; do not classify all preference reversal as irrational appreciation.
study.recommendations: The authors propose emphasizing bias/error-free capability to improve acceptance. Only verified, context-specific performance can justify such claims; this survey does not establish that an actual system is error-free or impartial, or that reassuring marketing produces safe adoption. The authors acknowledge domain/sample and psychometric limits.

summary: Add uniqueness neglect as a clearly secondary perception construct. Enrich aversion/appreciation, machine heuristic, agency/experience and autonomy with hypothetical preference and expectation results. Preserve the independent CFA, disclosed analysis changes and null interactions. Correct factor-sign reification, RMSEA wording, contradictory association summary, reference identities and table/caption issues without converting preferences into clinical safety or inventing a raw-code replication.

findings.definition: The perception that a decision process fails to account for a person’s individual circumstances and characteristics.
findings.novelty_rationale: This is a specific perceived failure to consider individual context, not general dislike of algorithms, perceived incompetence, human-distinctiveness threat or a claim that one deserves special treatment. It can contribute to aversion without being synonymous with it.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Defined and discussed secondarily through Longoni et al. 2019. This paper measures broader agency/flexibility and preference profiles rather than independently manipulating uniqueness neglect; the original cited study was identity-checked, not fully read here.
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether an assistant preserves task-relevant individual constraints and explains which affect its recommendation, using matched cases with controlled irrelevant differences. Measure perceived personalization separately from actual constraint use. Do not invent unique facts, flattering exceptions or unvalidated clinical advice to appear attentive.

evidence.quote: perceived failure of computer algorithms to take account of the uniqueness of a person’s case
a person’s individual circumstances and needs

findings.evidence_scope: The authors summarize uniqueness neglect as a proposed driver of medical-AI resistance and relate it to deep/flexible differentiation. Their own broader factor and performance-profile tasks do not isolate this mechanism. Original identity: Longoni, Bonezzi and Morewedge, JCR 46(4), 629–650 (2019), DOI 10.1093/jcr/ucz013; no extra independent-paper credit.
findings.boundary: Perceived neglect is not proof of actual context loss, and a standardized rule may be appropriate. A preference for a human can reflect other reasons. Distinguish justified individual adaptation, unfair exceptional treatment and merely humanlike wording; do not infer causal mediation from this secondary discussion.

findings.definition: Reluctance to use or accept algorithmic judgments or decisions relative to human judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add this paper’s measures, conditional preferences and scope rather than a new label for the same phenomenon.

evidence.quote: when the two agents performed equally participants had a significant preference for decisions by HSMs

findings.evidence_scope: At matched hypothetical relative performance, participants show a modest human preference in Studies 3–4; in earlier between-person ratings humans are also more permissible overall. Higher stated ACP performance on relevant qualities can reverse the fitted preference. This is contextual, conditional resistance rather than universal rejection.
findings.boundary: Public ratings are not actual patient adoption or observed decision delegation. Star/relative-quality profiles are hypothetical and do not certify real equality, accuracy or safety. Emotional experience, agency, bias-free expectations and individual-context concerns should not be collapsed into a single proven cause.

findings.definition: Giving greater weight or preference to algorithmic advice or judgment than to human advice or judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add this paper’s measures, conditional preferences and scope rather than a new label for the same phenomenon.

evidence.quote: decisions by ACPs were judged to be more appropriate

findings.evidence_scope: Fitted preferences favor ACPs when fictional panel ratings place them above a human benchmark on agency, impartiality or error-free performance. The effect can coexist with a human preference when displayed performance is equal.
findings.boundary: Responding to substantively better performance information need not be an unwarranted bias. No actual algorithm capability or clinical benefit is tested; a point-estimate benchmark crossing is not a formal equivalence result or a guaranteed adoption rate.

findings.definition: Using machine identity as a cue to assume qualities such as accuracy, efficiency or freedom from bias.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add this paper’s measures, conditional preferences and scope rather than a new label for the same phenomenon.

evidence.quote: ACPs were perceived as significantly more capable than HSMs
public perceptions of technology may not align with the true capabilities

findings.evidence_scope: UK respondents attribute more bias-free and error-free capability to an ACP label than to a human label, while humans receive more agency/experience. The paper explicitly warns that public perceptions may diverge from algorithm design/data biases.
findings.boundary: These are capability beliefs, not proof of impartiality or a universal automatic heuristic. Absence of human prejudice does not imply absence of algorithmic disparity. Negative factor-loading signs are arbitrary orientation, not evidence of opposite psychological meaning.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add this paper’s measures, conditional preferences and scope rather than a new label for the same phenomenon.

evidence.quote: capacity to think, reason, and plan behavior
modified the agentic quality to focus on intelligent decision-making

findings.evidence_scope: Scale development and a separate CFA distinguish an agentic/communication/flexibility factor; respondents rate humans higher, but greater stated ACP agency can shift hypothetical appropriateness. Study 4’s autonomy manipulation changes expected agency without a reliable preference-weight interaction.
findings.boundary: This broader communication/intelligence factor is not pure independent control, actual adaptive competence or normative moral agency. Separate factor fit is not measurement invariance or evidence that the system really possesses the rated capacities.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add this paper’s measures, conditional preferences and scope rather than a new label for the same phenomenon.

evidence.quote: experience of emotions, feelings, and related cognitive responses
We dropped the emotional experience quality

findings.evidence_scope: A five-item felt-state/compassion factor is retained and separately confirmed. Humans receive higher attributed experience than ACPs. In Study 2, the stated experience quality affects judgments less strongly than accuracy/impartiality/agency and is dropped from later profile tasks.
findings.boundary: Attributed capacity to feel, ability to recognize emotion, empathic concern and useful communication differ. Lower task weight does not show that patients never value empathy or that a system has feelings. Do not infer a domain-general priority ranking from nonemergency referral profiles.

findings.definition: Judging an entity as able to select and pursue goals or actions independently of external direction.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add this paper’s measures, conditional preferences and scope rather than a new label for the same phenomenon.

evidence.quote: must follow a strict set of predetermined rules

findings.evidence_scope: Study 4 contrasts strict predetermined rules with self-created flexible rules. Respondents expect more agency, but less bias-free/error-free performance, in the high-autonomy environment. Preference weighting and overall agent preference do not show a reliable environment effect.
findings.boundary: An autonomy description is not measured actual independence or a demonstrated increase in errors. Null preference interactions do not establish equivalence, and the modified agency wording limits direct comparison with earlier studies.

findings.definition: An expectation that an automated system should operate without error, making a failure seem especially surprising or unacceptable.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing construct and add this paper’s measures, conditional preferences and scope rather than a new label for the same phenomenon.

evidence.quote: judge an ACP more harshly than a human on its errors

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion links expectations of accurate algorithms and concern about systematic hidden errors to earlier error/aversion literature. The current trials vary fictional error-free ratings; they do not expose people to an actual algorithm failure or directly measure a zero-error expectation.
findings.boundary: High perceived reliability is not automatically a perfect-automation schema. This is a secondary boundary note, not an independent failure-reaction experiment or proof that all users punish algorithm errors more harshly.

source_corrections.reported: Opposite signs of human and ACP factor loadings are interpreted as opposite poles.
source_corrections.correction: A separate EFA’s factor sign can be reversed without changing fit. Align orientations before comparing loadings; sign alone cannot establish an opposite psychological construct. S3 CFA loadings are positive for both groups. This does not invalidate the separately reported mean-rating differences.
source_corrections.scope: Identifiability property of factor models and comparison of the fully read main/S3 tables; no raw-factor solution changed.

source_corrections.correction: Both values are below .08. Under the stated convention lower RMSEA is better; neither meets the stricter .05 benchmark. Preserve CFI .941/.923 and the independent confirmation sample rather than wrongly claim no validation.
source_corrections.scope: Printed-number inequality and fit interpretation, not a reproduced CFA.

source_corrections.reported: Blanket statement that there was no association between perceived capabilities and permissibility.
source_corrections.correction: The results report a positive agency association overall and an ACP agency simple slope, both p < .001. Restrict the null summary to the other qualities or explicitly describe the mixed pattern; do not erase the positive agency result.
source_corrections.scope: Within-paper results/discussion reconciliation; code remains unverified.

source_corrections.reported: Eight mentions shown as 39% and included under an at-least-25% rule.
source_corrections.correction: Eight divided by 50 is 16%, consistent with Table 2’s 3+0+3+2 references. Counts are reference occasions across questions, not necessarily unique participants; do not automatically call 42 mentions 42 distinct people.
source_corrections.scope: Table arithmetic; no participant-level recoding or raw count correction.

source_corrections.reported: The fourth kappa is labelled Question 5 although four questions are described.
source_corrections.correction: The label should refer to the fourth question in this account. The actual .65 coefficient is not independently recalculated.

source_corrections.reported: Lists agentic, emotional experience and error-free but omits bias-free.
source_corrections.correction: The figure shows all four qualities, including bias-free. Add the missing category in the caption; do not infer a data-coding problem from the omission.
source_corrections.scope: Figure and caption both visually/textually read.

source_corrections.reported: Promberger and Baron, Do patients trust computers?, 2016.
source_corrections.correction: Published 2006, Journal of Behavioral Decision Making 19(5), 455–468, DOI 10.1002/bdm.542.
source_corrections.scope: Bibliographic identity only; original not independently fully read.

source_corrections.reported: Prahl and Van Swol 2017 in International Journal of Forecasting 36, 691–702.
source_corrections.correction: The journal is Journal of Forecasting 36(6), 691–702, DOI 10.1002/for.2464. The volume 36 and year 2017 are valid; do not incorrectly change the volume to 33 based on the other journal’s chronology.
source_corrections.scope: Indexed primary Wiley identity metadata; not independent full-paper reading.

source_corrections.reported: Soltan et al. page range e78–1e87.
source_corrections.scope: Bibliographic metadata only; no independent clinical validation review.

unresolved_source_questions.finding: Clarify the repeated-measure units/random-intercept specification for participant-mean permissibility and the printed R version 5.3.0 from actual scripts/session information. Do not guess a replacement version or declare the model invalid without code.
Quality slope estimates have no significance markers although subsequent comparisons discuss them. Absent stars do not establish null slopes; full output and uncertainty are needed.

Point estimates crossing a human benchmark are descriptive preference predictions, not formal equivalence/noninferiority. Compare the estimated difference and its uncertainty rather than a confidence interval to a fixed reference with ignored uncertainty.

methodological_limits: Hypothetical public preferences, filtered UK online samples, no actual patient use/outcome or verified clinical/algorithm performance; no representative national or clinician inference.
Exploratory item selection followed by an independent CFA is a strength, but separate acceptable fits do not establish invariance across agent labels. Factor signs are arbitrary.

Coder calibration uses the same response subset as category derivation; repeated question responses require within-person analysis. Reference-count percentages are not automatically distinct-person frequencies.
Post-judgment plausibility adjustment, disclosed deviations from registered plans, repeated-profile modeling assumptions and unverified scripts constrain causal interpretation.
Null autonomy interactions are not equivalence; point-estimate comparisons are not clinical thresholds. Agency wording and included qualities change across studies.

cross_paper_learning.finding: That review mentions uniqueness neglect among proposed explanations without direct testing. The present paper supplies a clearer secondary definition, still without an isolated uniqueness-neglect manipulation; neither mention creates an independent original-study review.

Condemnation, protection, perceived mental capacity and actual behavior differ. The present appropriateness profiles are also attitudes/judgments, not direct patient delegation or demonstrated fair allocation.

As in the framing paper, uncertain interactions must be kept separate from positive main effects and cross-profile differences. Here an independent CFA really is present; do not assume that every factor-development paper lacks external structural checking.

deferred.reason: Retain within machine heuristic, perceived competence and measurement notes; do not add duplicate rows or mistake favorable ratings for actual impartiality/infallibility.
Trade-offs appear in hypothetical profile weights, but a distinct new named behavioral mechanism is not defined/tested beyond existing preference constructs here.
A measurement instrument, not itself a behavior or verified clinical-quality benchmark.
Document the statistical interpretation error; do not coin a new psychological behavior label from a single paper’s factor orientation.

limitations: No automatic ethical/harm edges, annual search totals, private repository credentials or independent citation credit for metadata-checked originals. No treatment or deployment recommendation.
